papers.title: Pop Goes the Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning of Voice Liveness Detection
papers.abstract: Many Automated Speaker Verification Systems (ASVs) commonly employ liveliness detection techniques, such as VoicePop, which identify genuine speech by analyzing low- frequency pop bursts from plosive phonemes using Gammatone Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (GFCC) and an SVM classifier. While effective against traditional replay attacks, such systems are vulnerable to data poisoning techniques. Prior work shows that broadly applied SyntheticPop attacks can collapse model to accuracy to as low as 14.01% using only 20% poisoned samples, but the resulting artifacts are easily detectable when visualizing the waveform energies. This paper introduces Pop Goes the Verifier, a stealthier phoneme injection poisoning attack. By leveraging FastSpeech 2 (FS2) with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder, we inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to reduce the visibility of injected artifacts in waveform and spectrogram analysis. Using the ASVSpoof 2019 as the dataset, we observe that the approach achieves a moderate poisoning attack while providing greater resistance to signal-level inspection than the original SyntheticPop attack.

papers.title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gslm2.

papers.title: Local or Escalate? Post-Training Expert Routing for Real-Time Duplex Speech Models
papers.abstract: A full-duplex model should answer easy questions immediately, but hard questions often need stronger reasoning, which may require waiting. The challenge is to choose between these paths at the moment the model begins to speak. Recent systems learn related mode decisions through special-token generation inside the dialogue model, coupling routing to turn-taking and temporally annotated full-duplex training. We study a post-training alternative. We freeze MiniCPM-o 4.5, using only its speech input and output, and fit a logistic failure readout on hidden states already available at its native listen-to-speak transition. The resulting gate requires no additional model generation and exposes thresholds that can be retuned without changing the duplex policy. A probe fitted on text-input states also reads the states of spoken questions, including unseen human recordings. On the internal benchmark, selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points. Compared with always using the expert, it reduces mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5 percent. It also outperforms matched random routing across external speech question-answering pools, as well as a zero-shot GPT-5.4 mini router that rates the transcribed question. The training recipe also transfers to a second duplex model family. These results show that an existing duplex model can be equipped to answer easy turns immediately and wait for stronger reasoning or fresher knowledge on the turns that need it, without further duplex training.

papers.title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
papers.abstract: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.

papers.title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.

papers.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
papers.abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

papers.title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://zhishengzheng.com/transdubber/.

papers.title: ResMamba: A Dual-Path Convolution-Mamba Model for Music Genre Classification
papers.abstract: Music genre classification remains a fundamental yet challenging task in music information retrieval, requiring models that capture local time--frequency patterns and long-range temporal dependencies. To address this, we propose ResMamba, a hybrid architecture that augments a ResNet-style four-stage backbone with Mamba blocks. Building upon the selective structured state space sequence model, ResMamba first adapts the selective SSM into a 4D-compatible residual Mamba block that captures global dependencies at linear complexity. We then design the ConvMamba dual-path block, which combines this adapted Mamba branch with a parallel convolutional branch through a learned $1\times1$ fusion, jointly modeling global sequential context and local spectro-temporal patterns. Furthermore, we adopt a multi-scale fusion head that aggregates hierarchical representations across all four stages. Experiments on the GTZAN dataset demonstrate that our full ResMamba model achieves a 5-fold cross-validation accuracy of $88.99\% \pm 1.58\%$, surpassing the strongest published method in our comparison (88.64\%). All models are trained from scratch without any pretraining, external data, or data augmentation. Beyond GTZAN, ResMamba also generalizes to the larger FMA benchmarks under the same training protocol, attaining $64.52\% \pm 1.88\%$ on FMA-Small under 10-fold cross-validation --- the best published from-scratch result --- and $65.75\%$ on FMA-Medium under the official artist-level split, surpassing the widely cited SVM baseline of Defferrard \textit{et al.} (63\%).

papers.title: Microphone Geometry Aware Regional Target Speaker Extraction
papers.abstract: Regional target speaker extraction (RSE) aims to extract speech originating from a specified angular region, relaxing the requirement for precise target speaker location when performing location based speech extraction. However, existing RSE methods typically assume a fixed microphone array configuration and microphone number, limiting their applicability to unseen microphone geometries and varying numbers of microphones. In this work, we propose a geometry-aware RSE framework capable of extract with varying microphone array geometry and microphone numbers. Specifically, we introduce an attention-based multichannel front-end to encode inter-microphone phase information, together with a spatial audio reconstruction-based auxiliary objective to improve the front-end spatial representations quality. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines across microphone arrays with four-microphones, while maintaining a performance gap of less than 0.6 dB compared with a tetrahedral geometry-specific baseline when evaluated on the tetrahedral microphone array.

papers.title: Wave Physics as Representation: Tensor-Structured Neural Reconstruction for Ocean Acoustic Fields
papers.abstract: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) complex ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements is challenging due to highly oscillatory wave structures and restricted sensing patterns/routes. Learning-based approaches fall into two categories. First, purely data-driven models can learn complex field patterns, but do not explicitly exploit wave physics that may enhance interpretability and reduce training costs. Second, physics-informed methods impose a specified physical equation as a reconstruction constraint, but often require environment-dependent parameters that are difficult to acquire. As a result, practical 3D acoustic field reconstruction that is both physically grounded and robust to uncertain environmental information remains largely unexplored. This work takes an alternative route: instead of solving a fully specified wave equation, it extracts a structured representation from wave physics and learns its components from data. From the Helmholtz equation and normal mode propagation, we derive a structured spatial-angular tensor representation, termed the S/c representation. Under a low-rank specialization, it takes the form of a rank-(L,L,1) block-term tensor decomposition, which connects structured sampling patterns/routes used in ocean sensing to sufficient conditions for field recovery. Building on this tensor representation, we propose TIDAL, a neural reconstructor that uses the S/c representation as an inductive bias for structured decoding and aligns information aggregation with the sampling geometry. The neural learner removes the need for known model parameters required by conventional physics-based recovery methods. Experiments across three structured sampling geometries show that TIDAL achieves the best reconstruction performance and fastest inference among baselines, with benefits from the physics-derived representation under limited data and model capacity.

papers.title: MEX: The Musical Expectation Benchmark Suite
papers.abstract: We propose the Musical Expectation (MEX) benchmark suite for perceptually validating computational models of musical expectation, i.e., models that estimate music information dynamics (MID) measures of perceived musical expectations, such as surprisal or uncertainty from symbolic music or musical audio. MEX collects and extends tasks for evaluating such models previously proposed in music information retrieval and cognitive sciences using standard datasets, and evaluates whether: (1) proposed MID measures decrease with repetition due to in-context learning of the computational model, (2) peaks in such measures align with boundaries of music segments, (3) pitch surprisal and uncertainty estimated from audio are consistent with those modeled in event-based symbolic music, (4) proposed MID measures can predict electrophysiological responses to music. We stress that this benchmark suite does not provide an exhaustive computational characterization of music expectation. Rather, we envision this as an active, interdisciplinary initiative, with benchmarks evolving as our understanding of the underlying perceptual processes deepens. We provide open-access code https://github.com/musicperceptmodeling/mex to estimate surprisal and uncertainty from audio using baseline models, run the tasks on standard datasets, and include utilities for running the tasks with users' own data.

papers.title: Spatial Transfusion: From Structured Spatial Scene Understanding to Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We formulate editing as a structured scene transformation over a taxonomy of atomic edits. Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, we introduce modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum that progressively adds generation, editing, and natural-language interaction. Experiments show that Spatial Transfusion largely preserves spatial understanding while outperforming full fine-tuning in generation and editing. The resulting model supports controllable FOA generation and editing through both structured and natural-language interfaces. Audio samples are available at https://microsoft.github.io/spatial-transfusion/

papers.title: InteractionBench: Measuring Timing, Task Accuracy, Whisper and Volume, and Grounding in Real-Time Voice Systems
papers.abstract: Most benchmarks for real-time voice systems focus on one aspect, such as turn-taking, instruction following, paralinguistic control, or conversational memory, each with its own data and set of systems. We present InteractionBench, a benchmark and evaluation harness that measures four dimensions on the same systems from the same recorded user audio: conversational timing, spoken-task accuracy, whisper and volume, and groundedness in conversations of more than twenty turns. The benchmark contains 221 items per system in thirteen scenarios. Before any system runs, we fix the expected floor-control actions for spoken tasks by rule and take the expected answers from scripted dialogues. We score whispering from the audio signal. We evaluate GPT-Live, GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live, Moshi, PersonaPlex, Freeze-Omni, and a turn-based cascade in 1,519 graded runs. Among the six full-duplex systems, timing and spoken-task accuracy are rank-correlated ($\rho = 0.83$), while the cascade has the highest spoken-task score (38/50) and the second-lowest timing score. No system corrects a user's grammar within the required window. Only Gemini Live whispers on most requests (8/10). Hosted systems pass 67-88% of groundedness probes, compared with 14-35% for open full-duplex models. Timing is measured where the client hears each system, so the timing of hosted systems includes network delay: for GPT-Live, whose server reports its own clock, removing a delay of about 1.5 s lowers its timing score from 86% to 56%. We also document where the protocol differs across systems, including the text instructions.

papers.title: VioTech: Frame-Level Violin Playing Technique Detection with Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Playing technique is crucial for expressive violin performance, yet few violin technique detection models exist. Current systems mainly rely on note-level pipelines that first estimate note boundaries and then classify techniques. This is especially problematic for bowed string instruments such as the violin, where soft onsets and continuous bow-string interaction render note segmentation unreliable. Here, we propose VioTech, a frame-level violin technique detection framework that predicts techniques directly at 10 ms resolution without explicit note segmentation. To handle the large temporal-scale variation among techniques, VioTech combines a frozen MERT encoder with a multi-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture and task-specific routing for tonal, articulation, and legato-related predictions. We also introduce VioTech120, the first manually annotated dataset of violin playing techniques constructed from real solo performance recordings, as well as an accompanying note-labeling user interface. Results demonstrate that VioTech achieved consistent improvements over prior methods and significantly enhanced cross-dataset generalization, establishing a new state-of-the-art in violin technique-aware transcription.

papers.title: Voice-Native LLMs Hear Frustration but Do Not Listen to It
papers.abstract: Users convey frustration in what they say and in how they say it, and voice-native models, which hear speech instead of an ASR transcript, can register both. Existing evaluations read unchanged performance as robustness without checking perception. Following Brunswik's lens model, we measure on identical audio whether frustration is expressed, perceived, and utilized. We cross frustrated wording with frustrated voice in a within-item 2x2 design over 353 tasks and release the 1,412 clips as VoxAffect. Across 8 models, outputs look robust, with no detectable vocal effect on accuracy for 7. With neutral wording, all 8 label the frustrated voice frustrated in at most 3.1% of clips, although 7 of them detect acted anger in 73-100% of clips and human listeners classify the voice correctly in 65.3% of judgments. Yet linear probes decode the frustrated voice from the audio encoders of the 2 open-weight models, with paired accuracy 0.67 and 0.69, and in proprietary models too the voice raises perceived frustration once the words agree. The models thus hear the frustrated voice but do not listen to it, whereas their invariance to frustrated wording, perceived in 40-75% of clips, is genuine robustness. Our work is openly accessible at https://github.com/Astarojth/hear-not-listen.

papers.title: ViSSFlow: Unifying Video-Conditioned Sound and Speech Generation via Joint Learning
papers.abstract: Video-conditioned audio generation, including Video-to-Sound (V2S) and Visual Text-to-Speech (VisualTTS), has traditionally been studied as two separate tasks despite their shared objective of generating audio conditioned on visual content. Existing methods rely on task-specific architectures and training paradigms, while the possibility of a unified generative framework remains largely unexplored due to heterogeneous conditioning signals and limited joint training data. In this paper, we propose ViSSFlow, a unified flow-matching framework for both V2S and VisualTTS. To effectively integrate diverse conditioning modalities within a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), we introduce a disentangled condition aggregation mechanism that exploits the complementary roles of attention layers, using cross-attention to model semantic conditions and self-attention to capture temporally dense visual cues. Furthermore, contrary to the common assumption that joint optimization of V2S and VisualTTS causes task interference, we show that a single model can be trained end-to-end without sacrificing task-specific performance. To address the scarcity of paired training data covering both sound and speech generation, we further propose a simple yet effective feature-level data synthesis strategy that enables robust joint learning. Extensive experiments on V2S, VisualTTS, and joint generation benchmarks demonstrate that ViSSFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art task-specific baselines while providing a unified solution for video-conditioned audio generation. Code and demos are provided in Supplementary Material.

papers.title: VoxServe: Streaming-Centric Serving System for Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech Language Models (SpeechLMs) are increasingly deployed for streaming speech generation, where audio playback must start quickly and never stall. Serving them requires running two very different model components on the same system. An autoregressive LLM backbone emits audio tokens, and a codec converts chunks of those tokens into waveforms. Existing systems run the two as separately scheduled stages, and therefore either serialize them, let them interfere, or strand capacity by placing them on separate devices. We observe that overlapping the backbone and the codec on separate parts of the GPU raises throughput. Although this increases codec latency, most chunks can tolerate it, as long as it neither lies on the critical path of time-to-first-audio (TTFA) nor causes a playback stall. Based on this insight, we present VoxServe, a SpeechLM serving system that allocates GPU resources according to the urgency of chunks. VoxServe executes work on three asynchronous lanes. The LM lane runs the backbone on a large partition of the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, the background codec lane runs on a small partition beside it, and the urgent lane uses the whole GPU. The scheduler queues each request to the LM lane and routes every chunk the backbone completes by its urgency. A request's first chunk and chunks close to their playback deadline go to the urgent lane, and the rest are batched on the background lane. On Qwen3-TTS, VoxServe sustains 1.5x the request rate of the best existing system at a 200ms TTFA target without playback stalls. The code of VoxServe is available at https://github.com/vox-serve/vox-serve.

papers.title: Benchmarking Language Modeling for Lossless Compression of Full-Fidelity Audio
papers.abstract: Autoregressive "language" models (LMs) trained on raw waveforms can be repurposed for lossless audio compression, but prior work is limited to 8-bit audio, leaving open whether such approaches work for practical settings (16/24-bit) and can compete with existing codecs. We benchmark LM-based compression on full-fidelity audio across diverse domains (music, speech, bioacoustics), sampling rates (16kHz-48kHz), and bit depths (8, 16, 24-bit). Standard sample-level tokenization becomes intractable at higher bit depths due to vocabulary size (65K for 16-bit; 16.7M for 24-bit). We propose Trilobyte, a byte-level tokenization schema for full resolution audio, improving vocabulary scaling from $O(2^{b})$ to $O(1)$ and enabling the first tractable 24-bit LM-based lossless compression. While LMs consistently outperform FLAC and yield state-of-the-art compression at 8-bit and 16-bit, we observe that compression gains become more modest as bit depth increases beyond 8-bit.

papers.title: Paediatric-HGNN: A Hybrid Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Detecting Disfluency in Children's Speech via Multiscale Acoustic Fusion
papers.abstract: Automated stuttering detection (ASD) systems struggle with paediatric speech due to high acoustic variability in developing voices and the subtle distinction between pathological stuttering and typical developmental disfluencies. We introduce Paediatric-HGNN, a framework using a Context-aware Part-whole Interaction Network (CaPIN) tailored for paediatric data. Instead of conventional 1D signal modelling, our approach builds a heterogeneous graph capturing hierarchical relationships between lexical units (word nodes) and fine-grained acoustic segments (frame nodes). Trained on curated paediatric corpora (UCLASS and FluencyBank), Paediatric-HGNN achieves 82.4% weighted accuracy and a Typical Disfluency F1-score of 0.386. Modelling hierarchical lexical-acoustic interactions captures developmental "searching" behaviour, offering a more robust and interpretable tool for early clinical intervention.

papers.title: Spatial DJ: Spatial Audio Control for Arbitrary Loudspeaker Layouts
papers.abstract: Object-based spatial audio promises render-anywhere playback, yet deploying it in a new venue still requires two tasks that are rarely addressed together: acquiring the physical loudspeaker geometry and enabling creators manipulate spatial audio while listening through the target loudspeaker system rather than a headphone proxy. We present Spatial DJ, a system for on-site loudspeaker layout acquisition and real-time spatial audio rendering and control, using head-worn AR in a coordinate frame aligned to the physical loudspeakers. In an 18-loudspeaker room, we evaluate calibration accuracy, repeatability, and control latency, and conduct an 18-participant listener study comparing diffuse and orbiting point-source rendering configurations applied to vocal and instrumental layers. Orbiting point-source conditions received higher ratings of perceived immersion, energy, and novelty than the diffuse baseline. Beyond this controlled setting, four representative deployments illustrate reuse of the same system across heterogeneous loudspeaker venues.

papers.title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
papers.abstract: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.

papers.title: Deployment-constrained key estimation with a DSP-guided transformer reranker
papers.abstract: Local music applications estimate key during library import and benefit from an analyzer that is small, fast, and runs in-process. We start from a compact chroma-template key analyzer that fits this budget but lags behind learned references. Learned systems reach higher accuracy, but their installed model and runtime dependencies can occupy tens to hundreds of megabytes. We present key lime, a 21.5k-parameter DSP-guided transformer reranker with a 115 KB model artifact and a 76.7 MB installed footprint, including the extracted ONNX Runtime. It adds 0.32 ms per track to deterministic DSP scoring. Trained from labels on 4,040 FMAK tracks, with 449 tracks for validation and 1,000 disjoint FMAKv2 tracks held out for evaluation, it improves MIREX from 61.08 to 73.55 +/- 0.46 and exact accuracy from 52.30 to 67.07 +/- 0.65 over three seeds (mean +/- population SD). It approaches a same-manifest local madmom KeyCNN reference at 74.16 MIREX. A 12-parameter circular input stage matches the accuracy range of a 468-parameter linear input projection.

papers.title: Mosquito acoustic identification at unseen recording sites: practical limits of common transfer remedies for vector surveillance
papers.abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring could widen mosquito surveillance, but a classifier trained under one set of recording conditions often fails when moved to a new site, device or enclosure. On a nine-species, five-condition corpus of about 271,000 recordings, the published baseline identifies species at 0.881 balanced accuracy under conditions it has seen and 0.175 under held-out ones. Using that corpus's leave-domain protocol, we asked which transfer strategy is most reliable when a program brings a new site online. Using fixed features from a pre-trained bioacoustic model and a small classifier improved held-out-condition balanced accuracy to 0.305, without updating backbone weights and in minutes of training per site. Four widely used additions did not improve transfer: rebalancing training across recording conditions, fine-tuning the backbone and fusing a weaker second modality each reduced accuracy, and a six-term objective reduced to a single alignment term. Rebalancing reversed direction across four encoders, helping weak representations and harming strong ones. Genus-level aggregation was more accurate than species-level classification (about 0.50 against 0.30), suggesting genus-level screening may be the more realistic operating point here. These results come from one corpus under one protocol, and are dataset-bounded guidance rather than validated general rules.

papers.title: SPHERE: A Multi-Attribute No-Reference metric for Binaural Speech Quality And Spatial Fidelity
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce SPHERE (Spatial and Perceptual Human Evaluation and Rating Estimator), a multidimensional no-reference perceptual evaluation framework for binaural speech. SPHERE defines nine distinct perceptual and spatial attributes that characterize the immersive listening experience. We detail the crowdsourcing protocol and evaluation template used to collect ground-truth human ratings. To demonstrate the tractability of automating this framework, we evaluate six baseline configurations across single-branch and Siamese architectures utilizing Mel-spectrograms, complex STFTs, and pretrained spatial embeddings (PhaseCoder). Experimental results demonstrate that these baseline estimators achieve strong correlation with human subjective ratings, proving the feasibility of automated multidimensional spatial audio quality assessment.

papers.title: Text-to-music Generation via Structured Captions AND Interpretable Evaluation
papers.abstract: Text descriptions of music are central to the performance of text-to-music generation (TTM) methods, but creation of paired text information for music generation is relatively under explored. Here, we propose training latent diffusion/flow-based music generation models conditioned on structured captions (SCAPs) and compare with typical free-form captions via a set of controlled ablations. We compare free-form vs. structured captions, partial vs. full information coverage, and global vs. temporal text information during training, by fine-tuning different configurations of a pretrained flow-based diffusion transformer (DiT) and using a multi-stage inference-time prompt rewriter. Further, we introduce a new text-alignment evaluation protocol inspired by Davidsonian Scene Graphs (DSGs) for a fine-grained, interpretable measure of faithfulness of TTM methods. With multiple metrics, we show 1) that fine-tuning our DiT on SCAPs significantly improves text-alignment on music generation outputs while also improving quality, and 2) our proposed Music DSG metric better correlates with human preference than CLAP.

papers.title: 8 Bits to End the Loudness War: Lossless Floating-Point Compression for Audio Streams
papers.abstract: We present a native extension to the Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) providing lossless compression for IEEE 754 single-precision (binary32) floating-point audio, alongside a survey and empirical benchmark of existing floating-point compression methods. While professional recording hardware increasingly adopts 32-bit float converters and digital audio workstations process sound exclusively in floating-point math, consumer distribution remains constrained to fixed-point integer PCM. Through Dynamic Positional Alignment (DPA), our implementation achieves approximately 44.1% compression ratios on natural multi-stage ADC recordings--matching the storage footprint of standard 24-bit integer FLAC--and approximately 60.2% on complex digital workstation masters. By preserving dynamic peaks beyond 0 dBFS, the format also allows listeners to undo clipping, providing a practical technical path away from the loudness war with virtually no storage overhead. We do not claim to introduce a fundamentally new compression paradigm; our approach is conceptually similar to the floating-point mechanism in WavPack (which remains undocumented in published literature). Instead, this paper compares existing methods, provides theoretical grounding for why they succeed or fail, benchmarks current codec implementations, and contributes a reference implementation of a proven method within the FLAC ecosystem.

papers.title: Rel2Traj: Inter-Source Relation-Aware Trajectory Generation for Text-To-Spatial-Audio
papers.abstract: "A car drives from front left to front right while a dog follows it." Such a description specifies no particular trajectory, yet imposes a constraint on the joint motion of both sources that must hold at every frame. Existing text-to-spatial-audio methods can position and move each sound source according to its description, but none of them ensures or verifies that such inter-source relations hold. We therefore propose Rel2Traj, which parses the description into sources, relations, and anchors, jointly generates the trajectories of all sources using a relation-conditioned diffusion model, and finally renders sounds from a pretrained text-to-audio model along these trajectories to produce binaural audio. For training and evaluation, we construct a synthetic dataset from a controlled language of source motions and inter-source relations. A single frame-wise relational geometry defines both our evaluation metric, the Relation Satisfaction Rate (RSR), and an auxiliary training loss. On motion-relation combinations held out from training, Rel2Traj maintains all relation types, whereas every baseline fails on at least one. A listening test further confirms that listeners recognize the described relations. To our knowledge, this is the first text-to-spatial-audio work to model relations among moving sources as explicit geometric constraints.

papers.title: GDBack: A Group-Delay Backdoor Attack on Speaker Identification via Analytic All-Pass Filtering
papers.abstract: Existing phase-based backdoor attacks on speaker identification rely on shared absolute phase patterns for cross-sample trigger consistency, while other audio backdoor attacks have explored shared transformations that produce input-dependent triggers. Whether phase-based triggers can achieve similar consistency without imposing identical output phase patterns remains unclear. We propose GDBack, a poison-only group-delay backdoor attack using cascaded second-order analytic all-pass filters. Applying a shared transformation across utterances ideally preserves spectral magnitude while introducing a consistent frequency-dependent phase response and group-delay contribution, without forcing identical output phases. Experiments on LibriSpeech and VoxCeleb1 with ECAPA-TDNN, x-vector, and RawNet3 achieve attack success rates above 94% across all six settings (97.00% on average), while maintaining benign accuracy close to clean models. Phase and magnitude interventions, inverse compensation, and parameter-sensitivity analyses support the role of the induced phase transformation in backdoor activation. Speech quality and content evaluations indicate limited perceptual and linguistic distortion, while robustness experiments, including real over-the-air tests, reveal varying effectiveness across conditions and architectures. These findings demonstrate that cross-sample trigger consistency can arise from a shared phase transformation without requiring a common absolute phase pattern.

papers.title: Spatially-Guided Speaker Extraction Based on Relative Position Cues
papers.abstract: We present a multi-channel target speaker extraction (TSE) framework that is guided by relative spatial cues rather than explicit speaker-dependent references, such as clean enrollment utterances or precise directions of arrival (DOA). The proposed approach encodes the target speaker through discrete, interpretable relations between concurrent speakers, such as left and right or near and far, referred to as the Relative Position Cue (RPC). This relational conditioning effectively leverages spatial information while avoiding explicit DOA estimation, thereby enabling more robust operation under realistic conditions. We evaluate the proposed method across multiple datasets encompassing diverse acoustic conditions, including directional and diffuse babble noise, varying numbers of microphones, mixtures with different numbers of speakers, and dynamic scenarios involving moving speakers. Experimental results demonstrate that the RPC-based approach consistently achieves strong extraction performance and generalizes well across all tested configurations, establishing it as a practical and interpretable alternative for spatially informed speaker extraction.

papers.title: High Frequency Safeguard and Weighted Objective Scoring Bandwidth Extension
papers.abstract: Speech Bandwidth Extension (BWE) reconstructs missing high frequencies from a band-limited signal. Please note that perceptually important information is often concentrated in short high-frequency (HF) events. Therefore, an effective BWE requires both accurate HF generation and explicit control over where, how often, and in what spectral form HF energy should be produced. To address the above HF supervision, we present HFSWO, a compact complex-spectral Swin-based dual-stream adversarial framework with two newly proposed specialized discriminators: 1. High-Frequency Safeguard Discriminator (HFSD) converts excessive framewise HF-energy ratios into a differentiable safeguard-constraint penalty optimized through a projected primal--dual augmented-Lagrangian update; 2. Weighted Objective Scoring Discriminator (WOSD) learns an interpretable convex objective scoring over spectral flatness, centroid, and rolloff. Our rigorous experiments on VCTK English and MLS French datasets across multiple frequency ranges, including noisy conditions, show significantly improved perceptual scores with 74.6% fewer parameters than the existing baseline AP-BWE, establishing a new baseline in the BWE task in multilingual and multispeaker setups.
